summary: Defines how to provide NetBIOS services in a TCP/IP environment, for both local networks and internetworks. It describes node types for different topologies, with or without IP broadcast, and explains the ideas and techniques in general terms. Detailed packet specifications are in the companion RFC 1002.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1001 explains how NetBIOS services can run over TCP and UDP. It describes the node types, support servers, and methods that the companion RFC specifies in packet-level detail.

subtitle: The concepts and methods for providing NetBIOS name, session, and datagram services over IP.

tldr.problem: NetBIOS defined a software interface rather than a common network protocol, so implementations did not necessarily interoperate and could not readily work across an internet.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC maps NetBIOS naming, sessions, and datagrams onto TCP and UDP, with B, P, and M end-nodes and NBNS and NBDD support servers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1001 is an Internet Standard describing concepts and methods. The packet formats and detailed procedures are in companion RFC 1002.

today: RFC 1001 is an Internet Standard published in March 1987. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it is read with RFC 1002 for packet details.

sections.title: NetBIOS Services and Their Purpose
sections.content:
NetBIOS provides a software interface for applications to find named resources and communicate. Because it did not define one official network protocol, implementations built on different foundations could fail to interoperate.

RFC 1001 specifies general methods for providing NetBIOS services over TCP and UDP, for local networks and internetworks. It covers name service, reliable sessions, and unreliable datagrams; companion RFC 1002 gives the detailed packet formats and constants.
sections.plainLanguage: NetBIOS lets applications find other resources by name, exchange reliable messages, or send datagrams. This RFC explains how those services use TCP and UDP.

sections.title: Design Principles
sections.content:
The design aims to preserve existing NetBIOS services, use existing standards without modifying them, minimize options, tolerate errors and unexpected shutdowns, and avoid requiring centralized management.

It also aims to limit broadcast traffic and require only the protocol elements needed for interoperability. Because computers may go offline without warning, name and session procedures must handle missing responses and retry where appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: The design reuses existing Internet protocols and tries to work when computers disappear without warning. It also limits unnecessary broadcasts and configuration requirements.

sections.title: End-Node Types and Support Servers
sections.content:
B nodes use local broadcasts and directed UDP and TCP, and can operate within one broadcast area without support servers. P nodes use only directed traffic and rely on servers. M nodes combine P-node behavior with broadcasts for faster local discovery, then use servers when needed.

The NetBIOS Name Server (NBNS) stores name and address information. The NetBIOS Datagram Distribution Server (NBDD) distributes group and broadcast datagrams where IP broadcast or multicast is not available.

The RFC defines local and internet topologies and recommends that a scope contain only B nodes or only P and M nodes. It warns that mixing B and M nodes in an internet can cause undetected name conflicts.
sections.plainLanguage: B nodes find names by broadcasting, while P nodes ask support servers. M nodes broadcast first and then use servers when they need more information.

sections.title: Scopes and NetBIOS Name Encoding
sections.content:
A NetBIOS scope is the population of computers among which a registered name is known. Its scope identifier is a string that meets domain-name requirements.

A NetBIOS name is 16 bytes at the application interface. First-level encoding splits each byte into two four-bit values, maps each value to an uppercase letter from A through P, and produces a 32-character name. The scope identifier is appended to form a domain-style name.

The protocol then uses the compressed domain-name representation described by the RFC's referenced DNS specification. This second-level encoding is used in packet formats, with one stated exception for node-status data.
sections.plainLanguage: A name is interpreted within its scope, which defines where the name is known. The protocol encodes each 16-byte name as 32 letters before adding its scope.

sections.title: Registering, Finding, and Releasing Names
sections.content:
Before use, a name must be registered and later defended against conflicting registrations. A name is unique to one owner or a group shared by multiple owners; that choice is made during registration.

B nodes broadcast registration and query requests. P nodes send them to the NBNS. M nodes try broadcasts first and continue with the P-node procedure if no local answer resolves the request.

The NBNS may operate as a bulletin board or actively challenge a recorded owner. It can assign a name lifetime and remove a registration if the node does not refresh it. A node that detects a name conflict must stop using the name except to delete it.
sections.plainLanguage: A node registers a name before using it, and other nodes can check who owns that name. The NBNS may check that an owner is still active and remove registrations that are not refreshed.

sections.title: Establishing and Closing Sessions
sections.content:
All node types use directed communication for the session service. A caller discovers the destination, opens a TCP connection to the well-known session port, and sends a request containing the calling and called names.

The receiver can accept the request, reject it, or retarget the caller to another IP address and TCP port. A retargeted caller opens a new connection and repeats session setup with the new destination.

After setup, the two applications exchange sequenced messages over TCP. Optional keep-alive packets can help detect a failed peer; closing normally attempts a graceful TCP close before aborting after a timeout.
sections.plainLanguage: A session starts with a TCP connection and a request naming both applications. The receiver accepts, rejects, or redirects the request before data messages are exchanged.

sections.title: Sending NetBIOS Datagrams
sections.content:
NetBIOS datagrams use UDP and do not guarantee delivery or order. A sender uses a unique name, group name, or broadcast destination; a B node broadcasts group and broadcast traffic within its local area.

P and M nodes use an NBDD to distribute group or broadcast datagrams, or may obtain the group members from the NBNS and send to them individually. Datagrams can be fragmented when they exceed the configured packet limit; RFC 1002 specifies the fragment fields.
sections.plainLanguage: A datagram is sent without setting up a reliable session, so delivery is not guaranteed. For group or broadcast traffic, P and M nodes use a distribution server or send to listed recipients.
